items.title: 10.10.2 Calculating the charge on an electron

blocks.text: A sample calculation uses a current of 0.20 A for 34 min. Mass of anode at the start 56.53 g, at the end 56.40 g, so the copper removed is 0.13 g. The charge passed is Q = I x t = 0.20 x 34 x 60 = 408 C. Since 0.13 g of copper requires 408 C, 1 g requires 408 / 0.13 C, and 63.5 g (1 mole) requires 408 / 0.13 x 63.5 = 99646 C. The electrolysis equation Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s) shows that 2 moles of electrons are needed per mole of copper. The charge on 1 mole of electrons = 63.5 / 0.13 x 408 C = 99646 C. With the charge on one electron 1.60 x 10^-19 C, L = 99646 / (1.60 x 10^-19) = 6.2 x 10^23 mol-1, in good agreement with the accurate value 6.02 x 10^23 mol-1.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book gives 408 / 0.13 x 63.5 = 99646 C for 63.5 g of copper; the product is 199292 C. Since 1 mole of copper needs 2 moles of electrons, the charge on 1 mole of electrons is 199292 / 2 = 99646 C, so L = 6.2 x 10^23 mol-1 is unchanged.
